description: Piaget in education: egocentrism, conservation, McGarrigle & Donaldson, and Hughes.
content_html:
Piaget in the Classroom

Piaget’s theory was not just an academic description of how children think — it had direct implications for education. If children at different ages are genuinely incapable of certain types of reasoning, then teaching them content that requires that reasoning is pointless. Piaget’s key educational message was: match what you teach to the stage of thinking the child has actually reached.

This influenced how schools are designed and how teachers plan lessons. Primary school classrooms with hands-on materials, practical activities and discovery learning all reflect Piaget’s insight that children at the concrete operational stage learn best through interaction with real objects, not through abstract explanation alone.

Egocentrism and Its Reduction

In the pre-operational stage, children are egocentric. This does not mean they are selfish — it means they genuinely cannot take the perspective of another person. Piaget demonstrated this with his ‘Three Mountains Task’, in which children were asked to describe what a doll placed on the other side of a model mountain range would see. Pre-operational children consistently described what they themselves could see, not what the doll’s position would show.

As children move into the concrete operational stage, egocentrism gradually reduces. They begin to understand that other people have different viewpoints, feelings and knowledge. This has important educational implications: collaborative group work, debate and perspective-taking activities become possible and valuable once children reach this stage.

Key Fact

Egocentrism (the inability to take another’s perspective) is characteristic of the pre-operational stage (2–7 years). It reduces as the child enters the concrete operational stage (7–11 years), enabling collaborative and perspective-taking activities in education.

The Development of Conservation

Conservation is the understanding that quantity does not change just because appearance does. Pre-operational children fail conservation tasks — they say a tall thin glass contains more water than a short wide glass even after watching the same water being poured between the two. They focus on the height of the water (what they can see) rather than reasoning about quantity.

Piaget believed children could not reliably pass conservation tasks until the concrete operational stage. In education, this means that until around age seven, lessons should not assume children understand that number, volume or mass are preserved across changes in arrangement or appearance.

McGarrigle and Donaldson’s naughty teddy study directly challenged Piaget’s claims about conservation. The aim was to investigate whether pre-operational children could demonstrate conservation when the change in arrangement was made accidentally rather than intentionally by an adult.

Method: Children aged between 4 and 6 were shown two rows of counters that were the same length. In the standard Piaget condition, the experimenter deliberately spread out one row and asked if there were now more counters. In the naughty teddy condition, a toy teddy ‘accidentally’ scattered one of the rows, and the same question was asked.

Results: In the standard condition, most children gave the incorrect answer (saying the longer row had more counters — matching Piaget’s findings). But in the naughty teddy condition, a much higher proportion of children gave the correct answer, saying the number was still the same.

Conclusion: McGarrigle and Donaldson concluded that Piaget had underestimated children’s conservation ability. When the change was accidental and natural, younger children could conserve — suggesting the issue was with Piaget’s task design rather than with the children’s cognitive capacity. The deliberate act of the experimenter spreading the counters may have signalled to children that something had changed, leading them to give the wrong answer.

Hughes’ policeman doll study challenged Piaget’s claims about egocentrism. The aim was to test whether pre-operational children could take another’s perspective when the task was made more meaningful and understandable.

Method: Hughes used a model with walls dividing it into sections, and placed two toy policemen dolls at various positions. He asked children to hide a boy doll so that neither policeman could see it. The task required the child to take the visual perspective of both policemen — a more complex perspective-taking challenge than Piaget’s Three Mountains Task, but also more meaningful because it had a real narrative purpose.

Results: Most of the children successfully hid the boy doll where neither policeman could see it, demonstrating that they could take the perspectives of the two policemen — something Piaget’s theory predicted they should not be able to do at this age.

Conclusion: Hughes concluded that pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed. When the task is meaningful and involves a familiar scenario (hiding from a policeman), even young children can take another’s perspective. This suggests Piaget’s Three Mountains Task was too abstract and unfamiliar, leading to an underestimate of children’s abilities.

Key Fact

Both McGarrigle and Donaldson (naughty teddy) and Hughes (policeman doll) found that children showed conservation and perspective-taking ability earlier than Piaget claimed, when tasks were made more natural and meaningful. Both studies challenge the idea that children’s thinking is as limited as Piaget’s original tasks suggested.

Implications for Education

The findings of McGarrigle and Donaldson, and Hughes, have important implications for how we understand and apply Piaget in education. If children are more capable than Piaget’s original tasks suggested, then earlier introduction of collaborative and perspective-based activities may be appropriate. However, Piaget’s core educational insight remains valid: the cognitive demands of a lesson should be matched to where the child actually is developmentally, not where a teacher assumes they should be.
exam_tip_html: For a ‘Describe a Study’ question on either McGarrigle and Donaldson or Hughes, structure your answer as aim, method, results, conclusion. Do not just describe the findings — you need all four elements for full marks. A common mistake is to describe the study but then draw a conclusion by referring to cultural or age differences rather than pointing to what the study itself showed — always tie your conclusion back to the specific results.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Piaget’s theory has direct educational applications: teaching should be matched to the child’s developmental stage, using hands-on activities in primary years and abstract work only from the formal operational stage.
  • McGarrigle and Donaldson’s naughty teddy study found that children could conserve when the change was accidental, suggesting Piaget underestimated conservation ability.
  • Hughes’ policeman doll study found children could take another’s perspective in a meaningful task, suggesting Piaget underestimated the age at which egocentrism reduces.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct conclusion from McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study?
A) Pre-operational children never understand conservation
B) Children showed better conservation ability when the change was accidental
C) The naughty teddy confused children and made them perform worse
D) Conservation is fully developed by age 4
practice_questions.marks: B) Children showed better conservation ability when the change was accidental [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by 'egocentrism' in Piaget's theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition capturing (1) the inability to take another's viewpoint/perspective, AND (2) linked to the pre-operational stage or the idea that the child assumes others see/think the same as them — e.g. 'The inability of a child in the pre-operational stage to appreciate that others have a different viewpoint from their own.' [2 marks].
Secure: Core idea correct but one element missing or vague [1 mark].
Developing: Partial — confuses egocentrism with selfishness only [0–1 mark].
Emerging: Incorrect [0 marks].

practice_questions.text: Describe how Piaget's theory can be applied to education.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Teaching should be matched to the child's developmental stage.
- Hands-on and practical learning suits the concrete operational stage (7–11).
- Abstract or hypothetical teaching is only appropriate from the formal operational stage (11+).
- Discovery learning: children should be allowed to explore and construct understanding themselves.
Mastering: Three clear applications linked to specific stages.
Secure: Two applications, one stage referenced.
Developing: General point about matching teaching to age.
Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one strength and one weakness of McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: The task was more naturalistic and child-friendly than Piaget's standard conservation task, making it more ecologically valid — children could respond naturally rather than second-guessing an adult's deliberate action.
Weakness: The naughty teddy condition may have distracted children with the 'naughty teddy' narrative, accidentally cueing the correct answer rather than testing pure cognitive ability — this reduces validity.
Mastering: Both strength and weakness developed with explanation of why.
Secure: Both identified, one developed.
Developing: One point, partially explained.
Emerging: One brief point.

Aim: To investigate whether pre-operational children could take another person's perspective when the task was more meaningful.
Method: A model divided by walls was used; two toy policemen were placed at positions within it. Children were asked to hide a boy doll so neither policeman could see it, requiring the child to take the visual perspective of both policemen.
Results: Most children successfully hid the doll in a position hidden from both policemen, demonstrating perspective-taking ability.
Conclusion: Pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed; when tasks are meaningful and involve an understandable scenario, even young children can take another's perspective.
Mastering: All four elements accurate and clearly stated.
Secure: Aim, results and conclusion present; method slightly vague.
Developing: Two elements; results or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Gist only.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate the challenge to Piaget's findings from McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study and Hughes' policeman doll study.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Piaget claimed pre-operational children lacked conservation and were egocentric.
- McGarrigle and Donaldson: naughty teddy scattered counters accidentally; more children conserved correctly than in Piaget's standard task.
- Hughes: children hid doll from two policemen correctly, demonstrating perspective-taking.
- Both suggest children are cognitively more capable earlier than Piaget claimed.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Strength of both studies: more ecologically valid — tasks were naturalistic and meaningful to children.
- Limitation: both used small or specific samples; may not generalise to all children.
- Counter to McGarrigle and Donaldson: the teddy narrative may have cued children, so results could reflect the fun of the game rather than true conservation ability.
- Counter to Hughes: the task was more complex (two policemen), which could mean children guessed correctly without true perspective-taking.
- Overall evaluation: Piaget's findings may have been task-dependent rather than stage-dependent; the challenges suggest stage boundaries are more flexible than Piaget believed.

Mastering: Both studies described accurately with elaborated evaluation.
Secure: Both described, two evaluation points.
Developing: One study described well, one evaluation point.
Emerging: One study described, no evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the key difference between the 'naughty teddy' condition and Piaget's standard conservation task in McGarrigle and Donaldson's study?
options: The naughty teddy task used liquid instead of counters
In the naughty teddy condition, the change was made to appear accidental
The naughty teddy condition had no experimenter present
In the naughty teddy condition, children were older

knowledge_checks.q: What did Hughes' policeman doll study conclude about Piaget's view of egocentrism?
options: Piaget was correct — pre-operational children cannot take another's perspective
Pre-operational children are more egocentric than Piaget claimed
Pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed when tasks are meaningful
Egocentrism does not exist in children under seven

knowledge_checks.q: McGarrigle and Donaldson found that children performed better on conservation tasks when the change to the counters appeared to be _____.
The ability to understand that quantity stays the same even when appearance changes is called _____.
Match each study to its key finding:
right: Children can conserve earlier when changes appear accidental
Children can take another's perspective in a meaningful task

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study?
flashcard_questions.a: To test if children could conserve when a change in arrangement appeared accidental rather than deliberate.

flashcard_questions.q: What did McGarrigle and Donaldson find in the naughty teddy condition?
flashcard_questions.a: More children correctly conserved when the teddy scattered counters accidentally than in Piaget's standard task.

flashcard_questions.q: What did McGarrigle and Donaldson conclude from the naughty teddy study?
flashcard_questions.a: Piaget underestimated children's conservation — task design affected results, not just cognitive stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the aim of Hughes' policeman doll study?
flashcard_questions.a: To test if pre-operational children could take another's perspective in a meaningful task.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Hughes find in the policeman doll study?
flashcard_questions.a: Most children successfully hid the doll so neither policeman could see it, showing perspective-taking ability.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Hughes conclude from the policeman doll study?
flashcard_questions.a: Pre-operational children are less egocentric than Piaget claimed when tasks are meaningful.

flashcard_questions.q: What is egocentrism in Piaget's theory?
flashcard_questions.a: The inability of a pre-operational child to see the world from another person's perspective.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the reduction of egocentrism matter in education?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows collaborative work and perspective-taking activities, which become possible in the concrete operational stage.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one limitation of both McGarrigle and Donaldson's and Hughes' studies?
flashcard_questions.a: Both used specific procedures that may have inadvertently cued correct answers, reducing validity.

flashcard_questions.q: Piaget used the _____ Task to demonstrate egocentrism in pre-operational children.
What educational implication follows from Piaget's idea that children's cognitive abilities develop in stages?
flashcard_questions.a: Teaching should be matched to the child's developmental stage, using concrete activities before abstract work.

glossary_terms.definition: Piaget's second stage of cognitive development (2–7 years), characterised by egocentric thinking and a lack of conservation.
In Piaget's theory, the inability of a pre-operational child to see the world from any perspective other than their own.
Piaget's third stage (7–11 years) in which children can think logically about concrete situations and show reduced egocentrism and acquired conservation.
The understanding that the amount or quantity of something stays the same even when its appearance changes.

glossary_terms.term: McGarrigle and Donaldson's naughty teddy study
glossary_terms.definition: A study by McGarrigle and Donaldson that challenged Piaget's conservation findings by making the task more naturalistic and child-friendly.
A study by Hughes that challenged Piaget's egocentrism findings by using a more meaningful and child-friendly perspective-taking task.

hero_image_caption: Children engage in hands-on tasks that reveal their real cognitive abilities.
